newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign crudes muted by slow demand and arb.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign crudes muted by slow demand and arb.

text.p: U.S. foreign crudes were subdued on Friday by slow refiner demand thinned by volatility from the Iraq crisis, and also tight Atlantic arbitrage.
Speculation that a Wall Street trader holding seven Brent stems had moved two cargoes into the U.S. Gulf could not be immediately verified.
Traders mostly agreed the arbitrage was uneconomic, but said the trader had booked a ship to load around Sept 23.
"If it was done, the price would've been between (Nov) WTI parity to minus 10 cents delivered," a Texas trader said, noting the WTI/Brent Nov arbitrage had fallen to $1.00/bbl.
The arbitrage was at $1.20 midweek, which had been deemed narrow although the softer Dated Brent market against 15-day Brent had offset the narrower spread.
But some traders said sales on larger vessels would still be profitable, although thin margins in the U.S. Gulf might not entice refiners to crank out incremental barrels.
In regional markets, Uruguay reportedly secured about a million barrels of Nigerian Forcados for November delivery at an undisclosed price, trade sources said.
No results were seen for Ecopetrol's short-term Cano Limon tender, but spot cargoes were pegged at WTI minus $1.60 fob.

In the aftermarket, Nov Brent partials traded between $23.12 to $23.05, reflecting a slightly weaker tone in line with Iraq stating it would halt attacks on U.S. jets patrolling U.S. "no-fly zones" in northern and southern Iraq.
Intermonth Oct/Nov Brent moved at plus 75 and 74 cents, also weaker than 80 cents traded earlier.
